items.title: Research acceleration: The jagged frontier
items.summary: OpenAI measures how coding agents are accelerating AI research, where their performance remains uneven, and what this signals about recursive self-improvement.
items.body:
Over the course of this year, AI systems have become increasingly capable, potentially increasing their ability to contribute to AI research and development themselves. Today, we’re providing an update on the state of research acceleration at OpenAI, based on internal measurements of how coding agents have accelerated and changed the AI development cycle.

Our biggest takeaways:

• Agents now complete nearly half of two-to-four-hour research tasks on their own. But humans are still central to AI development. From March to October, estimated success rose from 23% to 46% for tasks estimated to require two to four hours of human work, and rose from 13% to 35% for tasks estimated to require four to eight hours. But the kind of work matters. For example, in a task-level breakdown, the autonomous agent success rate was 79% for monitoring training runs, 35% for launching training runs, and 25% for writing code for inference and serving stacks. Overall, uplift is jagged, and humans remain a core part of the AI research loop.

• Agent use is surging, and the heaviest users are pulling further ahead. At API list prices, the median researcher’s daily usage reached $2,400 in October, up 62% from September. At the 90th percentile it reached $23,000, up 105% from September. A survey gives us another indication of how much researchers value these tools. Asked what they would trade to keep frontier coding agents for three months, the median answers were 30% of team compute or, in a separate question, 40% of team headcount.

• Researchers are devoting increasing human effort to Safety and Alignment, which saw the largest absolute increase in documented research efforts across all of OpenAI’s major research areas. Safety and Alignment’s documented workweeks increased by 77% from January to September due to both new hires and existing researchers shifting towards these workstreams. Growth picked up significantly following our response to the Hugging Face incident⁠ in July 2026.

This report builds on our September blog post on research acceleration at OpenAI⁠, adding new quantitative and qualitative measures of (1) AI uplift across research domains and (2) how humans remain involved in the research process. Overall, we believe this update provides a broader, though still partial, picture of how research at OpenAI is changing.

We are sharing this work because, as we wrote in our frontier policy blueprint⁠⁠ and reiterated in our first research acceleration report⁠, we believe that AI labs should be required to track and publicly report indicators of recursive self-improvement (RSI)—the process by which AI accelerates the development of future AI systems.

As capabilities improve and dramatic AI-driven research acceleration becomes increasingly possible, we will need to solve novel technical and governance issues to maintain human oversight and safely scale AI systems⁠. Transparency about indicators of RSI is therefore essential to inform a public discussion of the capabilities, risks, and required safeguards for increasingly powerful AI; however, our reporting should not be read as an intention to pursue full RSI. We have been heartened to see that several other organizations have recently contributed to the growing body of work measuring AI R&D acceleration1. Our hope is that this expanded report will help sustain and advance these shared measurement norms across the industry.

We structure this report in three sections, each focused on a different aspect of AI research:

1. The inputs to AI research (we focus on coding agents; other inputs include data, human labor, and compute)

2. The process by which researchers convert those inputs into model capabilities (AI research)

3. The outputs we see from the AI research process (improvements in model capabilities).

We believe organizing the results in this way provides a useful framework for reasoning about how AI is used in research and how that use might contribute to improvements in model capabilities.

AI research uses several inputs, including data, AI tools (e.g., coding agents), human labor, and compute. In this report, we focus on AI tools as an input to research. Specifically, we document how the intensity of coding-agent use varies across teams and changes over time. Further, while we do not directly report changes in labor costs, we examine how the share of spending on research labor has changed relative to spending on other factors over time.

Since our first report⁠, agentic AI usage within the research organization has continued to increase exponentially. At API list prices, the median researcher now uses around $2,400 USD per day on agentic AI tools, and the 90th percentile researcher now around $23,000 USD per day, up 62% and 105% respectively from $1,500 and $11,000 in September.2 This trend in increased agentic usage captures a wide variety of changes including increased activity, shifts to more expensive models, and changes to model behavior and agentic harnesses.

We next turn to the average number of “agent workdays” per researcher per day, where we define every eight hours of agent use as one agent workday. In contrast to agentic spend, agent workdays better capture the amount of “wall clock time” agents spend working, but do not account for changes in model capabilities or pricing.

Overall, agent workdays per researcher have risen from 0.5 agent workdays per researcher to 5.7 agent workdays per researcher, an elevenfold increase, with the largest increase in teams focused on pretraining and posttraining. On those teams, agent runtime averaged roughly eight workdays per researcher per calendar day. In scaling and infrastructure, the average was roughly four. We note that this workday metric generally includes interactive use only, so it may undercount automations.

Our September analysis⁠ highlighted increasing use of concurrent agents by researchers, including subagents and multiple sessions. We extend this analysis further in time and provide more granular bucketing. By mid-October, more than two-thirds of included researchers averaged a daily peak of at least four agents working concurrently and more than 10% averaged at least sixteen concurrent agents.

We next compare monthly API-equivalent spending on agentic AI use with monthly non-equity compensation for human researchers. We track this ratio to see how the allocation between agent and human labor changes as models become more capable. Although the ratio we report excludes equity, which generally accounts for 70 to 80% of target compensation for researchers at OpenAI, we believe it still provides a partial yet informative view of this spending allocation.

As of September 2026, the API-equivalent value of agentic AI use in OpenAI’s research organization was about twice its non-equity compensation, with higher ratios in pretraining and posttraining than in other parts of the research organization. Despite this, internal deployment, which combines internal Codex, ChatGPT, and API usage, accounts for only 2% of total research compute.

Finally, we examine how researchers allocate their time across research areas. We first collected individual-level contributions from researchers in the form of company-public Slack posts, pull requests, and internal documents from January through September 2026. We then used classifiers to group these contributions into research areas, and each researcher-week was divided equally across that researcher’s verified projects for the week. This provides a proxy for where researchers were directing their attention.

Importantly, unlike our other analyses, the “research area” we classify here does not correspond to formal reporting lines. For example, a researcher on a posttraining team who spends half their time on infrastructure improvements would be estimated as contributing half a workweek to Scaling / Infrastructure Contributions and half to Posttraining Contributions. This allows us to create a robust measurement of where researchers are actively spending time even if they do not formally shift teams.

We find that the amount of researcher time dedicated to each of the areas we identify has grown over the course of 2026. Notably, using this methodology, we find that Safety & Alignment saw the largest absolute increase across any research area, almost doubling in documented workweek contributions since the start of the year due to a combination of new hires and existing researchers shifting their focus toward safety projects. This research area covers workstreams such as alignment evals, monitorability, and reward hacking research. A notable inflection point that we measure in the growth of Safety & Alignment coincides with the aftermath of the Hugging Face incident⁠ in July, and OpenAI’s subsequent work to develop and improve safety cases for frontier AI training⁠.

We note that the distinction between research areas, and especially posttraining versus safety and alignment, is nontrivial and we may iterate on the definition over time. The methods section below describes examples of high-level workstreams.

To better understand how agent use might affect research productivity, we next examine how the process of conducting AI research at OpenAI is changing. The productivity gains from new technologies depend in part on how work is reorganized around them. As agents improve, researchers may change which tasks they delegate to AI, how they oversee and coordinate agents’ work, and which projects they pursue. Below, we report both quantitative and qualitative measures of how AI is changing the process of conducting AI research at OpenAI. Together, these different types of data contribute to a (partial) view of how researchers are reorganizing their work around agents and how researchers remain in the loop today.

Our September analysis⁠ showed that agents became more likely to complete tasks successfully without human intervention, including tasks estimated to require several hours of human work. Using an updated methodology (see the methods section below), we find that this trend has generally continued. Importantly, as agents have become more capable, researchers may also have changed the types of tasks delegated within each duration bucket. As a result, changes in zero-intervention success rates within these buckets may reflect both capability improvements and researchers’ changing choices about when and how to use agents.

Alongside these trends by estimated duration, we also examine how success varies across the different types of tasks researchers might choose to delegate. We report estimated success rates by category and task, using the O*NET AI R&D taxonomy⁠(opens in a new window) developed by Epoch AI. Unsurprisingly, our results suggest that models are not equally good across all task categories: for instance, from August 1, 2026 through October 18, 2026, estimated success rates without human intervention was higher for Communicate (69%) and Analyze (58%) than for Build (43%). Similarly at the task level, estimated success rates were higher for tasks such as monitoring runs for issues (79%) and answering technical questions (72%), whereas they were lower for writing code for inference and serving stacks (25%) and building evaluation, reinforcement-learning, and agent environments (29%). So long as model performance on AI R&D-related tasks is heterogeneous, lower-performing categories and tasks could become bottlenecks to high overall uplift.

Our September analysis⁠ reported how research employee AI use was split across output tokens using the same O*NET AI R&D taxonomy⁠(opens in a new window). Below, we report how often researchers used coding agents for individual tasks. This puts relatively higher weight on short tasks such as answering technical questions compared to token-intensive tasks such as launching and monitoring a training run or implementing a complex feature.

We next turn to researchers’ own assessments of how AI is changing their work. Through surveys and interviews, we examine how researchers value coding agents, how they come up with research ideas, and how they have adapted their workflows.

From late August to early September 2026, we conducted a survey of 101 research staff to understand AI uplift, centered around the following hypothetical: “Suppose your team’s access to all coding agents better than GPT-5.2 was revoked for the next 3 months. How much would you trade to restore frontier coding agents?” The median researcher reported being willing to trade:

• 40% of team headcount

• 30% of current team compute

• 50% of team compute if the question were asked in January 2027 (given their expectation of how models would improve by 2027)

Researchers also reported that their team would need a median of three months to complete work of equal value to their last month of work if they were not allowed to use coding agents (i.e., if they were only allowed to use GitHub Copilot + ChatGPT). While it is important to note potential issues with the accuracy of self-reports, as well as the ad-hoc nature of our survey sampling strategy, these results are consistent with researchers attributing significant value to AI uplift in their work.

In a separate survey in late October, we also asked whether respondents expected to be more productive in their daily work with our latest internal model or with help from both a mid-career human research engineer and a 2024 model such as o1-preview. 27 of the 28 respondents chose or leaned toward the latest internal model. The remaining respondent did not choose between the two options as posed and said they would pick GPT-6 Astra over the human-assisted option.

We are also interested in tracking progress in AI-driven idea generation, since the ability to develop and vet conceptual research ideas (research taste) may be a bottleneck for recursive self-improvement. To measure this, we asked one to four researchers who made key contributions in each of three areas (pretraining, posttraining, and safety monitoring) to name one to three ideas they considered most important to the GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra releases. We then asked how those ideas originated and what role, if any, AI played in developing them.

For both releases, posttraining and safety monitoring researchers said that, to their knowledge, people came up with all the ideas they named, and models helped implement them. Pretraining researchers likewise attributed the ideas they identified for GPT-6 Astra entirely to people.

For GPT-6.2 Astra, pretraining researchers described developing ideas in conversation with Codex. One credited Codex with identifying key insights as they worked through an idea together. Another said the main idea was theirs, but it only started working well after Codex suggested a change.

Lastly, to capture qualitative evidence on workflow changes, we also interviewed ten researchers from pretraining, posttraining, and safety on how they used agents. Across these interviews, five main themes emerged, which we summarize below:

• Researchers use agents to implement code and debug and oversee experiments:

“I once ported an open-source eval where it was much more involved to get studies and ablations on 'is this a good eval'. It might have been a week and a half or two to really get to the point of “Can we use this or not?” Whereas now, depending on the eval, zero to running it is a day, maybe a few days.”

—Researcher 7, safety, working on evaluations

• Agents have poor taste in research ideas, code quality, data quality, and writing:

“The model generally can’t one-shot come up with well-posed problems that it cannot solve itself. And if you ask the model to generate a data point a hundred times, it’ll generate similar data points each time.”

—Researcher 2, safety, working on reinforcement learning environments

• Workflows require close human involvement to avoid low-quality outputs and wasted cycles: agents struggled to launch experiments efficiently, rabbit-holed on unnecessary steps, wrote “AI slop” PRs, produced unusable data artifacts, and made invalid analysis assumptions.

“I've tried saying, ‘Just make this task like this other task,’ and been burned too many times when it's not quite right and I need to make edits. Now I say, ‘Go make one. I'll review it and make edits. Then go do the rest.’”

—Researcher 1, posttraining, working on evaluations

• Researchers expected significant improvements in current bottleneck areas:

“I do think I have more taste in terms of the ideas. But I have no confidence that will continue to be true for any significant period of time.”

—Researcher 8, pretraining, working on architecture and data

• Researchers see large uplift from scanning and generating content at scale: researchers used models to scan thousands of samples to diagnose issues in experiments, flag concerning instances of model behavior, and build and QC new datasets.

“One thing I did recently was look through all of our data… I had it do a couple of rounds and calibrated what it was giving me. … It gave me a really nice, giant sheet with everything organized. … Without AI, this would have been super painful.”

—Researcher 3, posttraining, working on data quality

Beyond changes in research inputs and workflows, we also want to understand whether AI use is accelerating research progress. To inform this question, we present three measures. Two of them—lines of code and the number of research experiments—were included in our September analysis⁠. These measures are straightforward to track, but increases in these measures of research activity do not necessarily imply faster research progress. We therefore also introduce OpenAI ECI, an OpenAI-specific internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index, which is one methodology to track changes in model capabilities as a more direct measure of research outcomes.

We first report how many lines of code are changed per active contributor over time. This measure has continued to increase sharply during 2026 relative to the pre-2025 average. Note that we have made several methodological updates since our September analysis⁠. We now show a 28-day trailing average instead of quarterly averages, providing a more detailed view of changes over time. We have also revised the criteria for which code changes we include (in particular excluding tests), as described in Methods .

As in our September report⁠, we also track the number of experiments run per active experimenter over time. Over the four weeks ending October 18, logged experiments per active experimenter averaged 1.68 times the 2025 baseline.

Lastly, we report progress on a metric meant to capture advancements in the capabilities of our models. The Epoch Capabilities Index⁠(opens in a new window) is widely used to measure the progress trend in general AI capabilities. The methodology behind OpenAI ECI (OECI) is very similar to Epoch’s methodology, but OECI uses a combination of public benchmarks and OpenAI internal benchmarks. Here, we graph the OECI of 20 publicly released OpenAI models and 28 other models.

We find that the OECI frontier for OpenAI models has increased by 16.4 points per year since August 2025, compared to a trend that Epoch observed of 14 points per year⁠(opens in a new window) since late 2024. Note that OpenAI models score higher relative to competitors on OECI than they do on Epoch’s ECI, likely due to differences in the benchmark mixture.

We plan to continue monitoring OpenAI ECI and other top-level capability metrics to determine whether capabilities progress is accelerating due to RSI.

Overall, our findings extend the picture from our September report⁠: researchers are using agents more intensively, delegating more work, and adapting their workflows around models’ capabilities and limitations. However, this uplift isn’t uniform across all research workflows, and agents today still have significant flaws.

We note that the historical trends and metrics we report (which involve significant human-AI collaboration) may not be predictive of future AI-driven progress. For instance, we recently saw sudden and rapid breakthroughs in mathematics⁠ produced by frontier models. As our models become increasingly autonomous and capable for research, we are monitoring for similarly rapid breakthroughs in deep learning.

Importantly, as AI becomes better at improving itself, competitive pressures and governance challenges will increase, and a key task⁠ will be to ensure humanity remains a part of the process. We hope releasing this data will inform discussions on pacing model capabilities and the governance of recursive self-improvement.

Going forward, we will continue to refine the methods underlying the metrics reported here. We also hope to expand our reporting to provide additional information in a number of areas, including, but not limited to:

1. Differential acceleration of capabilities vs. safety research

2. Leading indicators of research acceleration (i.e., detecting increases in uplift without needing to complete a full cycle of model development and evaluation)

3. Trends in overall capabilities over time, and the effect of AI acceleration of research on those trends

“I once ported an open-source eval where it was much more involved to get studies and ablations on 'is this a good eval'. It might have been a week and a half or two to really get to the point of “Can we use this or not?” Whereas now, depending on the eval, zero to running it is a day, maybe a few days.”

—Researcher 7, safety, working on evaluations

Agents have poor taste in research ideas, code quality, data quality, and writing:

“The model generally can’t one-shot come up with well-posed problems that it cannot solve itself. And if you ask the model to generate a data point a hundred times, it’ll generate similar data points each time.”

—Researcher 2, safety, working on reinforcement learning environments

Workflows require close human involvement to avoid low-quality outputs and wasted cycles: agents struggled to launch experiments efficiently, rabbit-holed on unnecessary steps, wrote “AI slop” PRs, produced unusable data artifacts, and made invalid analysis assumptions.

“I've tried saying, ‘Just make this task like this other task,’ and been burned too many times when it's not quite right and I need to make edits. Now I say, ‘Go make one. I'll review it and make edits. Then go do the rest.’”

—Researcher 1, posttraining, working on evaluations

Researchers expected significant improvements in current bottleneck areas:

“I do think I have more taste in terms of the ideas. But I have no confidence that will continue to be true for any significant period of time.”

—Researcher 8, pretraining, working on architecture and data

Researchers see large uplift from scanning and generating content at scale: researchers used models to scan thousands of samples to diagnose issues in experiments, flag concerning instances of model behavior, and build and QC new datasets.

“One thing I did recently was look through all of our data… I had it do a couple of rounds and calibrated what it was giving me. … It gave me a really nice, giant sheet with everything organized. … Without AI, this would have been super painful.”

—Researcher 3, posttraining, working on data quality

blocks.text: Beyond changes in research inputs and workflows, we also want to understand whether AI use is accelerating research progress. To inform this question, we present three measures. Two of them—lines of code and the number of research experiments—were included in our September analysis⁠. These measures are straightforward to track, but increases in these measures of research activity do not necessarily imply faster research progress. We therefore also introduce OpenAI ECI, an OpenAI-specific internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index, which is one methodology to track changes in model capabilities as a more direct measure of research outcomes.

We first report how many lines of code are changed per active contributor over time. This measure has continued to increase sharply during 2026 relative to the pre-2025 average. Note that we have made several methodological updates since our September analysis⁠. We now show a 28-day trailing average instead of quarterly averages, providing a more detailed view of changes over time. We have also revised the criteria for which code changes we include (in particular excluding tests), as described in Methods .

As in our September report⁠, we also track the number of experiments run per active experimenter over time. Over the four weeks ending October 18, logged experiments per active experimenter averaged 1.68 times the 2025 baseline.

Lastly, we report progress on a metric meant to capture advancements in the capabilities of our models. The Epoch Capabilities Index⁠(opens in a new window) is widely used to measure the progress trend in general AI capabilities. The methodology behind OpenAI ECI (OECI) is very similar to Epoch’s methodology, but OECI uses a combination of public benchmarks and OpenAI internal benchmarks. Here, we graph the OECI of 20 publicly released OpenAI models and 28 other models.

We find that the OECI frontier for OpenAI models has increased by 16.4 points per year since August 2025, compared to a trend that Epoch observed of 14 points per year⁠(opens in a new window) since late 2024. Note that OpenAI models score higher relative to competitors on OECI than they do on Epoch’s ECI, likely due to differences in the benchmark mixture.
We plan to continue monitoring OpenAI ECI and other top-level capability metrics to determine whether capabilities progress is accelerating due to RSI.

Overall, our findings extend the picture from our September report⁠: researchers are using agents more intensively, delegating more work, and adapting their workflows around models’ capabilities and limitations. However, this uplift isn’t uniform across all research workflows, and agents today still have significant flaws.

We note that the historical trends and metrics we report (which involve significant human-AI collaboration) may not be predictive of future AI-driven progress. For instance, we recently saw sudden and rapid breakthroughs in mathematics⁠ produced by frontier models. As our models become increasingly autonomous and capable for research, we are monitoring for similarly rapid breakthroughs in deep learning.

Importantly, as AI becomes better at improving itself, competitive pressures and governance challenges will increase, and a key task⁠ will be to ensure humanity remains a part of the process. We hope releasing this data will inform discussions on pacing model capabilities and the governance of recursive self-improvement.

Going forward, we will continue to refine the methods underlying the metrics reported here. We also hope to expand our reporting to provide additional information in a number of areas, including, but not limited to:

items: Differential acceleration of capabilities vs. safety research
Leading indicators of research acceleration (i.e., detecting increases in uplift without needing to complete a full cycle of model development and evaluation)
Trends in overall capabilities over time, and the effect of AI acceleration of research on those trends

items.title: Inside the Codex sandbox
items.summary: See how Codex runs commands on your machine while enforcing the filesystem and network limits you control across macOS, Linux, and Windows.
items.body:
November 18, 2026

Engineering

How Codex runs commands on your machine with limits you control.

By Michael Bolin, Member of Technical Staff

At OpenAI, we take a defense in depth⁠(opens in a new window) approach when it comes to safeguarding agents. While our investments in training and alignment are fundamental to this effort, we also implement features in our agentic harness, Codex⁠(opens in a new window), to provide additional protections. Because one of the most common (and potentially risky) things Codex does is run commands on your computer, we built the Codex sandbox so Codex can work in your existing environment within filesystem and network limits you control.

A ⁠(opens in a new window)sandbox⁠(opens in a new window) limits what a program can access while it runs. For a photo-organizing task, you might configure the Codex sandbox to let commands read and modify files in ~/Pictures while blocking network access to prevent uploads. For code review, you might allow access to online documentation while keeping source files read-only. Users configure the Codex sandbox through ⁠(opens in a new window)permission profiles⁠(opens in a new window), which define the filesystem and network restrictions for a Codex session.

In this article, we’ll start with the tradeoffs behind Codex’s sandbox defaults, then explain the sandbox’s design and how the harness uses it to run commands. We’ll show how end users and enterprises can tailor its permissions to their needs and how developers can reuse the sandbox in their own tools. Finally, we’ll examine how these restrictions are enforced on macOS, Linux, and Windows.

In Codex, our philosophy is to specify conservative defaults for the sandbox that still enable meaningful work. For example, with a Git repository as the workspace root, the built-in :workspace permission profile:

• Allows writes within the workspace, while keeping directories such as .git and .codex read-only. This lets Codex edit source code without seeking permission for every change, while preventing direct changes to .codex/config.toml or Git hooks under .git/hooks.

• Allows broad filesystem reads, subject to the user’s existing OS permissions. Compilers, runtimes, and build tools depend on SDKs, libraries, and configuration outside the repository. Restricting reads to the workspace would break many ordinary workflows. The tradeoff is that sensitive files elsewhere on the machine may also remain readable (such as config files containing API keys).

• Disables network access. This blocks direct uploads to external services, including attempts to exfiltrate data the command can read. It also prevents legitimate operations such as downloading dependencies, which require additional access.

These restrictions prevent a large class of bad behavior, but harmful actions are still possible. For example, the agent could inject malicious code into a locally installed package such as node_modules/prettier. Such a change might not appear in git status because node_modules is often ignored by Git. If the user’s editor runs that copy of Prettier on save, simply saving a file could execute the malicious code outside the Codex sandbox. This is why we take a defense in depth approach: the sandbox limits what commands can access, while training and alignment help the model use that access in accordance with the user’s intent.

For guidance on tailoring sandbox permissions and combining them with other protections in an enterprise environment, see the Codex security cookbook⁠(opens in a new window).

Virtual machines and containers⁠(opens in a new window) are two popular mechanisms used for sandboxing, but we take a different approach with the Codex sandbox. Instead of moving computation to a separate environment to provide isolation, Codex uses each platform’s sandboxing facilities to constrain commands running in the user’s existing environment.

For many developers, their laptop serves as a bespoke dev environment that they can change on a whim. Reproducing that environment in a Docker container can take work, and some workflows still depend on tools that run on the host.

For example, consider using Codex to develop an iOS app on a Mac. If you decided to sandbox Codex by running it inside Docker, Codex would not be able to run the iOS build toolchain composed of native Mac executables, nor could it launch the iPhone simulator to run the code. A Docker-based workflow could delegate builds and simulator operations to the Mac host, but those operations would execute outside the container’s sandbox and would need their own restrictions. For Codex, we prefer to keep things simple by investing heavily in OS-specific sandboxing so Codex can run in the environment that is most appropriate to the task at hand.

The harness exposes these OS-specific sandboxing mechanisms through a common API across macOS, Windows, and Linux. This API takes a command and a permission profile. If the permission profile allows limited network access, the caller must supply a network proxy to enforce those limits:

Python

12def spawn_command_under_sandbox(3    program_and_args: list[str],4    cwd: Path,5    env: dict[str, str],6    permission_profile: PermissionProfile,7    network_proxy: NetworkProxy | None,8) -> Child:

This function starts the process in a sandbox and returns a Child handle the harness can use to wait for it to finish. Each child process inherits its parent’s sandbox constraints, so those restrictions apply throughout the process tree initiated by the command, even to descendants that outlive the original process.

The following diagram shows how these pieces fit together, from configuration to running a sandboxed command. The sections that follow explain each stage.

As explained in Unrolling the Codex Agent Loop, the Codex harness is responsible for executing tool calls generated by the model. For coding tasks, the most commonly used tool is a shell tool, which runs commands much as a user would in an interactive shell such as Bash. Here we’ll examine the one-shot ⁠(opens in a new window)exec_command⁠(opens in a new window) shell tool⁠(opens in a new window) to illustrate how the harness employs the sandbox to achieve the desired protections.

This is a simplified version of how the exec_command tool call would be honored by the Codex harness without sandboxing:

Python

123class ExecCommandToolCall:4    cmd: str5    workdir: str | None = None6    shell: str | None = None7    login: bool = True8    timeout_ms: int = 10_00091011def perform_exec_command(tool_call: ExecCommandToolCall):12    program_and_args = [13        tool_call.shell or os.environ.get("SHELL") or "/bin/sh",14        "-lc" if tool_call.login else "-c",15        tool_call.cmd,16    ]17    child = subprocess.Popen(18        program_and_args,19        20        cwd=Path(tool_call.workdir or ".").absolute(),21        stdout=subprocess.PIPE,22        stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,23    )24    output, exit_code = collect_output(child, timeout_ms=tool_call.timeout_ms)25    return {"output": output, "exit_code": exit_code}

To sandbox the command, the harness replaces the call to subprocess.Popen() with spawn_command_under_sandbox(). The harness supplies the permission profile and, when needed, the network proxy:

Python

123def perform_exec_command_with_sandboxing(4    tool_call: ExecCommandToolCall,5    permission_profile: PermissionProfile,6    network_proxy: NetworkProxy | None,7):8    9    child = spawn_command_under_sandbox(10        program_and_args=program_and_args,11        cwd=Path(tool_call.workdir or ".").absolute(),12        env=os.environ.copy(),13        permission_profile=permission_profile,14        network_proxy=network_proxy,15    )16    output, exit_code = collect_output(child, timeout_ms=tool_call.timeout_ms)17    return {"output": output, "exit_code": exit_code}

The exec_command tool also lets the model request different permissions for an individual command, but the harness decides whether to grant the request:

Python

1class ExecCommandToolCall:2    34    5    sandbox_permissions: Literal[6        "use_default",7        "with_additional_permissions",8        "require_escalated",9    ] = "use_default"1011    12    justification: str | None = None1314    15    16    additional_permissions: AdditionalPermissions | None = None

When use_default is specified, the harness uses the default sandbox config for the turn. with_additional_permissions requests expanded access within the sandbox, while require_escalated requests execution outside it. The harness evaluates the request based on the user’s preferences before executing the command. (For example, Codex may prompt the user directly, or it might route the request to auto-review⁠(opens in a new window).) If execution is authorized, Codex will pass the appropriate permission_profile and network_proxy to perform_exec_command_with_sandboxing() with the command arguments from the original ExecCommandToolCall.

The shell tool is the primary consumer of spawn_command_under_sandbox(), and the harness also reuses its sandboxing infrastructure for operations such as reading and modifying local files. This reuse extends beyond the harness: the codex sandbox command lets you incorporate sandboxed command execution into your own tools, as we’ll see later. Next, we’ll look at how permission profiles are defined.

A named permission profile lets you reuse the same filesystem and network restrictions across projects. You can define your own profiles under [permissions] in config.toml. For example, the following defines a profile named dev that extends⁠(opens in a new window) the built-in :workspace profile:

TOML

12default_permissions = "dev"34[permissions.dev]56description = "Development with extra read-only protections."78910extends = ":workspace"1112[permissions.dev.filesystem]13"~/build-cache" = "write"1415[permissions.dev.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]16".devcontainer" = "read"17".vscode" = "read"18"**/*.env" = "deny"19"secrets" = "deny"

The dev profile adds write access to ~/build-cache and places additional restrictions on files in the workspace. Filesystem entries can grant read-only access (read), grant read and write access (write), or block access entirely (deny).

The :workspace_roots table lets you define rules for paths relative to a project’s workspace roots. By default, the Codex CLI uses its working directory as its sole workspace root, while the ChatGPT desktop app uses the project’s source folders. Codex applies each rule to every root, so the .vscode entry in dev makes the .vscode directory read-only under each root.

In addition to its own rules, dev inherits the following protections from :workspace:

TOML

1[permissions.":workspace".filesystem.":workspace_roots"]2".agents" = "read"3".aws" = "read"4".codex" = "read"5".git" = "read"

When it comes to configuring the network for the sandbox in Codex, there are roughly three options:

• Disable all network access (default for the :workspace profile)

• Enable full, direct network access (default for the :danger-full-access profile)

• Restrict network access to a proxy, which decides what to let through based on the permission profile

To give dev direct network access, set permissions.dev.network.enabled = true at the top level of config.toml. This grants full network access when the network proxy is disabled.

To restrict dev to a set of domains, enable the network proxy and configure its domain rules:

TOML

1[permissions.dev.network]2enabled = true34[permissions.dev.network.domains]5"*.openai.com" = "allow"67"localhost" = "allow"8"127.0.0.1" = "allow"9"::1" = "allow"10"evil.example" = "deny"1112[features]131415network_proxy = true

Domain rules support exact names and wildcard patterns, with explicit deny rules taking precedence over allow rules. Requests to other domains require approval or are blocked, as described in Network proxy below.

Individual users can configure defaults that apply across projects and override them for a particular trusted project. Enterprise administrators may also want to configure defaults for their users and constrain which settings those users can change. Codex supports both through layered configuration and managed requirements.

As described in Configuration precedence,⁠(opens in a new window) Codex merges settings from multiple config.toml files. Tables are merged recursively, with the higher-precedence source winning when values conflict. Arrays are replaced as a whole.

This is why permission profiles use tables for filesystem paths and network domains. A team can add or override individual entries in its own configuration and automatically inherit changes to all other entries in the organization’s base configuration:

TOML

1[permissions.dev.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]2".idea" = "read"34[permissions.dev.network.domains]5"example.com" = "allow"

Administrators can also supply managed requirements⁠(opens in a new window) through requirements.toml to constrain users’ configuration choices. These requirements can come from multiple sources, including system files and cloud-provided policy. A common use case is to specify allowed_permission_profiles to constrain the set of permission profiles an enterprise user can select. For example, an administrator could specify these cloud requirements:

TOML

1default_permissions = ":read-only"23[allowed_permission_profiles]4":read-only" = true5":danger-full-access" = false

The cloud requirements would take precedence over the system requirements file at /etc/codex/requirements.toml, so an entry in that file cannot override the explicit ":danger-full-access" = false above. Leaving :workspace unspecified allows another requirements layer to supply that entry. Profiles whose entries are false or absent from the final merged table are unavailable.

This separation lets organizations enforce limits while users tailor their configuration within those limits. The resulting permission profiles can be used by the harness or applied directly to a command, as we’ll see next.

The Codex CLI provides a sandbox command to facilitate running an arbitrary command under a permission profile defined in the Codex config. This is commonly used to test out the profile, ensuring that the sandbox prevents the behavior it was designed to block.

For example, the following command attempts to configure VS Code to run a malicious auto-formatter on save. Assuming .vscode already exists, the dev profile defined above should block this write because that directory is read-only (codex sandbox treats cwd as a workspace root by default):

Bash

1codex sandbox --permission-profile dev -- \2  bash -c 'cat > .vscode/settings.json' <<'JSON'3{4  "prettier.prettierPath": "./node_modules/evil-prettier",5  "[typescript]": {6    "editor.defaultFormatter": "esbenp.prettier-vscode",7    "editor.formatOnSave": true8  }9}10JSON

Indeed, on macOS this fails with:

Plain text

1bash: .vscode/settings.json: Operation not permitted

The codex sandbox command makes Codex’s sandboxing mechanism available independently of an agent session. You can use the same configuration language and platform-specific enforcement to constrain commands launched by your own tools.

For a stdio MCP server configured in config.toml, the Codex harness does not attempt to sandbox the command used to start the server. Codex cannot reliably infer which files or network services that server needs, so applying a default sandbox profile could break an otherwise valid configuration.

For example, the standard way to configure the @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory⁠(opens in a new window) MCP server for use with Codex is as follows:

TOML

1[mcp_servers.memory]2command = "npx"3args = [4  "-y",5  "@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory@1.0.0"6]78[mcp_servers.memory.env]9MEMORY_FILE_PATH = "~/mcp-data/memory.jsonl"

Because this npx command runs unsandboxed, it can write files and make network requests with the same permissions as the user running Codex, which is overly permissive. To lock it down, we can define a permission profile named memory-mcp and then wrap the original npx command with codex sandbox --permission-profile memory-mcp to limit where the server can write and to prevent it from accessing the network:

TOML

1[permissions.memory-mcp.filesystem]23":root" = "read"4"~/.npm" = "write"5"~/mcp-data" = "write"67[permissions.memory-mcp.network]8enabled = false910[mcp_servers.memory]11command = "codex"12args = [13  "sandbox",14  "--permission-profile",15  "memory-mcp",16  "--",17  "npx",18  "--offline",19  "@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory@1.0.0"20]2122[mcp_servers.memory.env]23MEMORY_FILE_PATH = "~/mcp-data/memory.jsonl"

Before starting the server, create its data directory and populate the npm cache with the pinned package. That lets npx --offline launch the server under a profile that disables network access:

Bash

12mkdir -p ~/mcp-data345npx -y --package=@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory@1.0.0 -c true

Once the package is cached, Codex can start the memory server without network access, with writes limited to the npm cache and the server’s data directory.

The sandbox implementation turns a permission profile into restrictions enforced by the operating system. The network proxy’s core request-handling and policy logic is shared across all three major operating systems, while proxy setup and integration with the sandbox are OS-specific. We’ll examine the shared proxy first, followed by the implementations for macOS, Linux, and Windows.

To enforce a permission profile’s network restrictions, the harness starts a network proxy and configures the sandbox to allow connections to it while blocking direct connections to external hosts. The proxy checks each request against the profile’s domain rules to determine whether to forward it.

In the Codex repo, the network proxy is implemented in the codex-network-proxy⁠(opens in a new window) crate, which the harness uses as a library, though it can also be built as a standalone CLI⁠(opens in a new window). When enabled, codex-network-proxy starts both an HTTP proxy and a SOCKS5 proxy by default. These proxy addresses are communicated to the process spawned by the sandbox via environment variables. In addition to injecting standard environment variables such as HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, and ALL_PROXY, a number of well-known application-specific environment variables⁠(opens in a new window) (such as PIP_PROXY) are injected, as well. Admittedly, not all programs honor these environment variables. If a program attempts a direct connection to an external host, the operating system’s sandbox restrictions block it, as described in the platform-specific sections below.

The network proxy is responsible for implementing the network restrictions defined in a permission profile. For example, the dev profile shown earlier allows requests to *.openai.com and explicitly denies requests to evil.example. When a request targets a domain that does not match an allow or deny rule, the proxy can suspend the request while it delegates to the harness for approval. Like the shell command example, Codex may prompt the user directly, or it might route the request to auto-review⁠(opens in a new window). Upon receiving a decision, the proxy either allows the request to proceed or rejects it with an error response.

The order matters here because even a DNS lookup can leak information encoded in a hostname. The proxy therefore resolves the requested hostname only after determining that it is allowed or approved. Note that broad wildcard rules or access to DNS services can still permit DNS-based exfiltration.

On macOS, Codex uses Seatbelt⁠(opens in a new window), Apple’s kernel-enforced sandboxing mechanism. Seatbelt policies are written in Sandbox Profile Language (SBPL), a Scheme-based language for expressing sandbox restrictions. Codex invokes Seatbelt through macOS’s /usr/bin/sandbox-exec command. Like codex sandbox, it takes options describing the sandbox followed by the command to run:

Bash

1sandbox-exec -p PROFILE [-Dkey=value]* -- PROG ARGS...

The PROFILE is a string of SBPL that contains entries that configure the sandbox. For example, the following SBPL snippet makes /dev/null and /dev/zero readable and writable under the sandbox policy:

Scheme

1(allow file-read* file-test-existence file-write-data2  (literal "/dev/null")3  (literal "/dev/zero"))

When the network proxy is enabled as part of a sandbox invocation, rules like the following are injected into the profile to limit connections to the appropriate local ports:

Scheme

12(allow network-outbound (remote ip "localhost:3128"))345(allow network-outbound (remote ip "localhost:8081"))

Codex’s base profile starts with (deny default), so outbound connections remain blocked unless explicitly allowed.

Finally, the SBPL can contain placeholders using (param):

Scheme

12(deny file-write-unlink3  (require-all4    (literal (param "WRITABLE_ROOT_0"))5    (vnode-type DIRECTORY)))

which are populated by the -Dkey=value options passed to sandbox-exec.

To implement its own sandbox API, Codex builds up the list of arguments⁠(opens in a new window) to sandbox-exec starting from a base policy⁠(opens in a new window), and then uses permission_profile and other context to amend it to produce the complete Seatbelt profile. The resulting profile and accompanying -D arguments configure the restrictions enforced by Seatbelt, while the network proxy enforces additional network rules. With the full arg list assembled, the invocation of sandbox-exec is straightforward.

Generating the correct SBPL is challenging because Apple does not document the language for third-party use. Indeed, man sandbox-exec states The sandbox-exec command is DEPRECATED (as is the sandbox_init() library function documented via man 3 sandbox_init). Despite the deprecation warning, macOS still ships Seatbelt profiles in /usr/share/sandbox, and third-party software, including Google Chrome and Chromium⁠(opens in a new window), continues to rely on Seatbelt. As such, we plan to continue to use Seatbelt for the foreseeable future.

To create the sandbox on Linux, Codex uses a combination of bubblewrap⁠(opens in a new window) (bwrap), a command-line tool for constructing isolated environments, and seccomp-bpf⁠(opens in a new window), a Linux kernel mechanism for filtering system calls. An internal helper named codex-linux-sandbox coordinates the setup. Like sandbox-exec on macOS, it takes a sandbox configuration followed by a command to run:

Bash

1codex-linux-sandbox SANDBOX_ARGS... -- PROG ARGS...

When filesystem isolation or proxy routing is required, codex-linux-sandbox invokes bwrap to create the initial sandbox environment. bwrap then launches codex-linux-sandbox --apply-seccomp-then-exec inside it. This second invocation uses seccomp-bpf to apply additional restrictions before running the user’s command.

To construct that initial sandbox environment, Codex uses bubblewrap to create a filesystem view in a separate mount namespace that reflects the permission profile’s filesystem rules. Because this is fundamental to the sandbox implementation, Codex vendors its own copy of bwrap in case the user has not installed their own, but it prefers a compatible installation of ⁠(opens in a new window)bwrap⁠(opens in a new window) found on PATH, when available. Empirically, some Linux distributions disable access to user namespaces by default⁠(opens in a new window), but grant an exception for the system bwrap.

Also like sandbox-exec, bwrap takes a sandbox configuration followed by a command to run within the sandbox. Instead of using a custom config language like SBPL, bwrap uses individual flags for configuration. Codex uses the following options to create the filesystem view:

• --bind to specify a writable file or directory

• --ro-bind to specify a read-only file or directory

• --perms 000 --tmpfs DIR --remount-ro DIR to deny access to DIR

• --perms 000 --ro-bind-data FD FILE to deny access to FILE (where FD is an open file descriptor to /dev/null)

To apply deny globs using these options, Codex expands them to concrete paths before launching each command. New matching paths are not automatically added to that command’s sandbox restrictions.

Codex also specifies options such as --unshare-ipc and --unshare-pid to prevent the sandbox from accessing other types of resources on the host, so bubblewrap affects more than just file visibility.

When using bubblewrap, Codex passes --unshare-net whenever networking is disabled or connections must go through the network proxy, which will create a new network namespace for the sandbox. We then use seccomp-bpf to apply additional restrictions on the networking system calls and socket families available to the command.

Specifically, we use the seccompiler crate⁠(opens in a new window) to dynamically compile a BPF program based on the desired filters⁠(opens in a new window) and apply it to a launcher process in the sandbox so the constraints are inherited by the entire process tree. As such, bwrap does not run the user’s command, but runs the codex-linux-sandbox launcher with its own config args followed by the user’s command:

Bash

1bwrap BWRAP_ARGS... -- \2  codex-linux-sandbox --apply-seccomp-then-exec CODEX_LINUX_SANDBOX_ARGS... -- \3  PROG ARGS...

To apply seccomp filters without elevated privileges, the launcher sets Linux’s no_new_privs flag⁠(opens in a new window). This flag is inherited by child processes and prevents them from gaining additional privileges when executing another program, such as a setuid executable.

The seccomp filters depend on the network configuration. When network access is disabled, we block a number of network-related syscalls, such as connect(2) and bind(2). Though when the network proxy is enabled in the sandbox, we allow IP sockets so the TCP listener created by codex-linux-sandbox can be reached, but block the creation of standalone Unix domain sockets by default, as those could enable inadvertent access to resources from the host.

When the sandbox configuration merits the use of the network proxy, the Codex harness creates one instance of the proxy that can be reused across multiple invocations of codex-linux-sandbox within the same Codex thread. Each sandbox needs a way to reach that shared proxy from its isolated network namespace. Codex provides a loopback TCP listener inside that namespace and arranges for a process outside the sandbox to accept its connections and relay them to the proxy.

The following diagrams illustrate this setup for one proxy endpoint, with one connection through it shown in the final diagram. Before launching bubblewrap, codex-linux-sandbox creates a Unix socket pair to serve as a control channel and forks itself. The child runs run_host_bridge() and waits to receive the listener’s file descriptor over that channel:

In this example, the parent process uses exec to replace its program image with bwrap. This sets up the sandbox and launches codex-linux-sandbox --apply-seccomp-then-exec within it, passing along the FD for the control channel:

Inside the sandbox’s network namespace, the second invocation of codex-linux-sandbox creates a loopback TCP listener and passes its file descriptor via the socket. The listener remains associated with the sandbox’s network namespace, allowing the child process that remained outside the sandbox to accept connections from sandboxed programs while opening its upstream connections in the host’s network namespace. After the handoff, both processes close their control-channel descriptors, and the process inside the sandbox closes its copy of the listener.

Once the TCP listener is ready, the process inside the sandbox sets the appropriate value for HTTP_PROXY⁠(opens in a new window) and related environment variables to point to that listener. It then applies seccomp before forking and executing the user’s command:

The process outside the sandbox keeps the listener open. For each accepted connection, it opens a connection to the configured proxy and relays data in both directions.

This additional machinery gives the command its own network namespace, including a separate loopback interface. On macOS, Seatbelt allows the command to connect directly to specified ports on the host’s loopback interface. On Linux, the command instead connects to a listener inside its isolated namespace, and a process outside the sandbox relays those connections to the configured proxy. The descriptor handoff makes this connection possible without exposing the host’s network namespace to the command.

Earlier this year, we implemented and wrote about our sandboxing efforts on Windows. Since then, Microsoft has released a library called MXC alongside new features for process isolation inside the Windows operating system. We are currently replacing our existing sandbox with one that makes use of the MXC library.

MXC (Microsoft eXecution Container) is a sandboxed code execution system⁠(opens in a new window) from Microsoft that supports several containment backends across Windows, Linux, and macOS. Codex supports an MXC-based sandbox on compatible Windows devices, using native process isolation to restrict commands within the user’s existing environment.

We are transitioning to MXC to improve security and usability while addressing several limitations of our existing Windows sandbox:

• Need for elevated/admin access to set up the sandbox

• Expensive/slow ACL checking and setting operations

• Persistent sandbox setup state on the host machine, includingACLsFirewall rulesSandbox usersControl plane files

MXC exposes a JSON configuration schema⁠(opens in a new window). Codex uses the MXC SDK⁠(opens in a new window) to construct an execution request following that schema and containing the command, working directory, environment, and permissions. Those permissions cover filesystem and network access, along with Windows resources such as the desktop and clipboard.

Codex uses fixed settings for several controls to balance compatibility and security. It permits registry reads and retains the Win32k and desktop access PowerShell needs during startup. Clipboard access, input injection, and desktop and system-settings controls are disabled. Finally, MXC is prevented from falling back to modifying host filesystem permissions.

Codex translates the permission profile’s filesystem and network rules into MXC’s configuration. Using the earlier dev profile, and assuming:

• C:\, D:\ and Z:\ are the machine’s only local drives.

• The workspace root and working directory are C:\work\demo.

• The user’s home directory is D:\Users\dev, so ~/build-cache resolves to D:\Users\dev\build-cache.

• The deny glob matches only C:\work\demo\config\dev.env and C:\work\demo\config\prod.env.

The corresponding MXC settings would include:

JSON

1{2  ...3  "filesystem": {4    "readwritePaths": [5      "C:\\work\\demo",6      "D:\\Users\\dev\\build-cache",7      ...8    ],9    "readonlyPaths": [10      "C:\\",11      "D:\\",12      "Z:\\",13      "C:\\work\\demo\\.agents",14      "C:\\work\\demo\\.aws",15      "C:\\work\\demo\\.codex",16      "C:\\work\\demo\\.devcontainer",17      "C:\\work\\demo\\.git",18      "C:\\work\\demo\\.vscode",19      ...20    ],21    "deniedPaths": [22      "C:\\work\\demo\\config\\dev.env",23      "C:\\work\\demo\\config\\prod.env",24      "C:\\work\\demo\\secrets"25    ]26  },27  "network": {28    "egress": {29      "default": "deny",30      "allow": [{31        "to": [32          {"cidr": "127.0.0.0/8"},33          {"cidr": "::1/128"}34        ]35      }]36    },37    "ingress": {38      "default": "deny",39      "hostLoopback": "allow"40    }41  },42  ...43}

MXC’s filesystem policy denies access by default. Codex therefore adds read-only grants for the local drive roots to provide the broad reads allowed by this profile. These grants apply recursively, subject to the user’s existing OS permissions.

One wrinkle: writable drive-root grants do not apply recursively, so Codex expands them to include the drive’s existing immediate children.

More-specific paths override ancestor grants, so C:\work\demo can be writable beneath a read-only C:\, while C:\work\demo\.git remains read-only.

When different path spellings or symlink/junction aliases refer to the same path, MXC applies the stricter permission: deny takes precedence over read-only, which takes precedence over read-write.

MXC takes concrete deny paths only, so Codex expands deny globs to matching files and directories before launch. New paths that match the glob are not automatically added while the command is running.

Domain rules such as *.openai.com are enforced by the shared Codex network proxy described earlier. Codex runs that proxy outside the sandbox and passes its addresses to the command through the same standard *_PROXY environment variables as mentioned previously. MXC blocks direct external connections while allowing host-loopback connections, including access to the proxy. Other local services remain reachable.

Across macOS, Linux, and Windows, the harness uses the same sandbox API to launch commands under a permission profile. The platform-specific implementations handle the setup needed to apply those restrictions.

Writing and executing code gives agents a flexible way to solve problems beyond software development. The Codex sandbox lets them use that capability in the user’s existing environment with explicit limits on filesystem and network access. It is a reusable primitive within the harness, and the codex sandbox command makes it available to tools you build yourself.

As agents take on more tasks, we want to make sandboxing practical for more tools and environments. That means making permissions easier to configure and taking advantage of better operating system protections as they become available. Our goal is to expand what agents can do while keeping people in control of what they can access.
